Issued at 304 AM CDT Thu Aug 13 2026

A very broad and shallow upper level ridge extends from an upper
trough over the Pacific Northwest to another trough over the
northeast U.S. The apex of the ridge is currently situated
around eastern Montana. Latest satellite imagery shows an upper
level jet laying over the northern Great Lakes region with
current isolated convection over central ND associated with the
entrance region of this jet. Additional isolated convection over
central and into northeast Montana is associated with another
impulse lifting northeast through central MT, approaching the
apex of the ridge. With this broad upper flow over the area
today scattered showers and isolated thunderstorms will be
possible. However, the general thinking is that the current  
convection in central ND will wane with the diurnal temperature 
minimum and as the Great Lakes wave continues exiting to the 
east. Scattered showers and isolated thunderstorms may linger 
this morning in the northwest to north central ahead of the next
approaching wave, but with upper level ridging expected over 
the state today, the confidence in shower/thunderstorm activity 
beyond this morning is low. Will maintain some low to medium 
pops today mainly in the west through north central as CAMS do 
indicate some shower activity with mainly light qpf amounts. 
The main show will be late tonight through Friday.

Upper level flow around the northwest U.S upper low will direct
moisture from the central Pacific, across the Desert Southwest 
and eventually into the northern High Plains. In addition, a 
subtropical mid level high over the Gulf of America will allow 
gulf moisture to work its way northward into the Northern 
Plains. By 12Z Friday NAEFS PW anomalies in excess of the 99th 
percentile are situated over the Montana and North Dakota border
and track northeast across northwest North Dakota during the 
day Friday. In addition, ECMWF EFI values in excess of 80 
percent are situated over northeast Montana into northwest North
Dakota for the period centered on 12Z Friday, with a shift of 
tails in excess of 2 in the far west, north of the Missouri 
River (indicating an elevated probability of an extreme event). 
Thursday night a mid-level impulse lifts into eastern Montana, 
then across western and into north central ND during the day 
Friday as a surface low over southeast Montana with an inverted 
trough into northeast Montana, lifts into north central ND by 
00Z Saturday. Although the overall instability is not great 
during this timeframe, there should be enough forcing from the 
approaching shortwave, combined with the resulting surface 
cyclogenesis and FG forcing to produce some rather significant 
precipitation amounts. The NBM 24 hour probability (06Z Friday 
to 06Z Saturday) of an inch of QPF is greater than 70 percent 
over far northwest ND, and greater than 50 percent from northern
McKenzie county into western Bottineau county. The probability 
of 2 inches of QPF during that same timeframe ranges from 
around 30 to 60 percent in far northwest ND. Looking at some 
heavy rain parameters for Crosby around 12Z Friday, we see a 
PWAT in excess of 1.50", mean RH around 90 percent and warm 
cloud depth in excess of 11,000 ft, all very favorable 
parameters for heavy rain. A couple of negative factors are the 
lack of instability giving us that tall skinny CAPE, and a 
rather progressive MBE movement. One thing to note was that 
early in the period (late Thursday into early Friday) when you 
may have better potential for stronger convection with heavy 
rain, is when MBE movement is greatest. You may have 
thunderstorms with very high rainfall rates, but they may be 
moving rather quick. Later in the period, say during the day 
Friday, as the surface low tracks slowly northeast through 
western ND, the MBE movements slow down. Thus you may not have 
the excessive rainfall rates from stronger convection, but the 
movement of the system as a whole slows. From a winter 
perspective there is a quite impressive signature of very strong
Omega, 2D FG forcing and deformation to the north of the 
surface low on Friday. Looking at the HREF PMM and LPMM 24 hour 
qpf, you can make out a couple bands of high qpf. One over 
northeast MT and far northwest ND, possibly associated with the 
stronger convection, and another tracking more from west central
into north central ND, possibly associated with the slower MBE 
movement. Both produce some locally heavy rain amounts in excess
of 3 inches. 

Of course there's plenty of time for this scenario to shift 
east or west or break down or intensify. We will definitely need
to monitor. Given our dry summer so far, an areal flood watch 
is not in the forefront of our minds, but if this scenario 
holds, it's a possibility that we may need some headlines for 
excessive rainfall. WPC has the northwest in a slight risk for 
excessive rain. Stay tuned.

After Friday we dry out over the weekend. Temperatures Tod
